title: Rigidity of an algebraic field tower with one rational endpoint
statement: Let $k,K,L$ be fields [def-weil-field], with $k$ algebraically closed [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $i:k\to K$ and $\alpha:K\to L$ be unital field homomorphisms [def-pc-field-extension], and set $j=\alpha\circ i:k\to L$. Assume that $L$ is algebraic over $K$ through $\alpha$: each $z\in L$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial with coefficients in $\alpha(K)$. If either $i$ or $j$ is bijective, then all three specified maps $i,j,\alpha$ are bijective. The conclusion concerns these maps, not merely abstract isomorphisms between the fields.

source.place: Tags 09GQ (definition-algebraically-closed) and 09GR (lemma-algebraically-closed), triviality of algebraic extensions; the two-alternative tower argument is the expansion of old Step 3 of lem-trf-etale-completed-local-ring-iso.

proof.text: All three specified maps are injective, by [def-pc-field-extension]. Explicitly, if a unital field homomorphism $f$ killed a nonzero $a$, then $1=f(a)f(a^{-1})=0$, impossible in its target field; applying this to a difference gives injectivity. It therefore remains to prove surjectivity in the two alternatives.

source.place: Tags 09GQ (definition-algebraically-closed) and 09GR (lemma-algebraically-closed); elementary assembly for the specified tower maps

proof.text: Suppose $i$ is bijective. Fix $z\in L$. Algebraicity supplies a nonzero $P(T)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\alpha(b_r)T^r$ with $b_r\in K$ and $P(z)=0$. Choose $a_r\in k$ with $i(a_r)=b_r$ and put $Q(T)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}a_rT^r$. Then $P(T)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}j(a_r)T^r$ because $j=\alpha\circ i$. Some coefficient of $P$ is nonzero, so the corresponding $a_r$ is nonzero; thus $Q\ne0$ and $z$ is algebraic over $k$ through $j$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-over-algebraically-closed-subfield] with its $k'=k$, its target field $k=L$, its homomorphism $\alpha=j$, and its element $x=z$. Its algebraic-closedness hypothesis is precisely the hypothesis on our $k$, and the required algebraicity is the equation just obtained. Hence $z=j(a)$ for some $a\in k$. This proves $j$ surjective and also $\alpha$ surjective, since $z=\alpha(i(a))$. Together with Step 1 and the assumed bijectivity of $i$, all three maps are bijective.

source.place: Tags 09GQ (definition-algebraically-closed) and 09GR (lemma-algebraically-closed); elementary assembly for the specified tower maps

proof.text: Suppose instead that $j$ is bijective. For each $z\in L$, choose $a\in k$ with $j(a)=z$; then $z=\alpha(i(a))$, proving surjectivity of $\alpha$. For each $b\in K$, choose $a\in k$ with $j(a)=\alpha(b)$. The equality $\alpha(i(a))=\alpha(b)$ and the injectivity of $\alpha$ from Step 1 imply $i(a)=b$, proving surjectivity of $i$. Step 1 now gives bijectivity of $i$ and $\alpha$, while $j$ was assumed bijective. This case needs neither algebraicity nor algebraic closedness.
